newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE - Brazil Bahia a surprise fiscal role model.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Brazil Bahia a surprise fiscal role model.

text.p: Brazil has finally taken on the multi-billion dollar task of helping spend-thrifty states break loose from the shackles of ever-increasing debt.
But as the billions fly, it will be one of those states that does not need to crawl on bended knees to the capital Brasilia that will probably stand out.

Poor Bahia, more often than not the butt of jokes from its rich cousins in the industrial south, is ironically a shining beacon of fiscal well-being among the chaos of the public finances of Brazilian states.

"We certainly set an example that even Brasilia could follow," gushes Rodolpho Tourinho Neto, finance-secretary of the northeastern state, better known for golden beaches and a languid pace of life than for financial credibility.

Of Brazil's 27 states (including the federal district), about 12 are thought to be virtually bankrupt, unable to repay federal loans and struggling to cover payroll costs. The total net debt of the states and municipalities stood at 83.99 billion reais ($82.3 billion) in July, up from 81.926 billion reais in June.
SALVAGE PROGRAMME STARTED LAST MONTH
In mid-September, Finance Minister Pedro Malan started signing the first deals to salvage the states' finances.

Brasilia agreed to refinance six billion reais of the debt of the southern state of Rio Grande do Sul in return for fiscal adjustments, a voluntary redundancy plan and a commitment to retire 20 percent of its huge debt stock through asset sales.
And it signed up to an 8.6 billion-real refinancing plan for Minas Gerais with the same conditions.

Pedro Parente, the finance ministry's executive secretary, told Reuters the substitution of old short-term debt paying unbearably high rates with 30-year federal paper paying just six percent a year will allow interest finally to be paid.

It also halts the inexorable rise in the debt stock because the states' enormous payroll costs -- 87 percent of total net receipts in Rio Grande do Sul -- meant they were having to take out further debt just to meet their basic obligations.
The next customers are likely to be Rio de Janeiro with five billion reais and Mato Grosso do Sul with 2.2 billion reais.
But Bahia is not expected to have to beg the federal government to help it out of any fiscal quagmire, because despite its poverty, Bahia's finances are apparently healthy.
BAHIA HAS CUT PAYROLL COSTS

Neto and Bahia state Governor Paulo Ganem Souto says a fiscal adjustment plan begun in 1991 has cut payroll costs to below 60 percent of net receipts, the limit set constitutionally but rarely observed by other states.

Bahia's debt is just over four billion reais with projected 1996 net annual receipts at 3.3 billion. Debt-servicing costs in 1996 are expected to be 12.2 percent of net receipts. Rio Grande do Sul's debt is about twice annual net receipts.
Bahia owes no money to private banks and has no short-term debt contracts, known as Anticipated Budgetary Receipts (AROs), which pay cripplingly-high rates.

"In 1991, our finances were a mess, we were unable to pay anything," Neto told Reuters in the Bahian capital Salvador. "We realised we had to be able to live off our own resources and began a radical adjustment plan."

The plan involved cutting state secretariats to 13 from 23, introducing a voluntary redundancy programme in non-core areas, which has already cut 7,000 jobs from the state's 190,000-strong payroll, and privatisations.
The state trimmed the sort of salary distortions that have seen police colonels retire as millionaires elsewhere. "Super salaries don't exist here," Governor Souto states categorically.

Bahia mothballed its loss-making ferryboat crisscrossing Salvador's Bay of All Saints and put the service out to tender. It has sold off its stakes in the petrochemical sector and it is planning to privatise next year the state energy firm COELBA.
Eventually, the government hopes to auction concessions to run major roads and to sell its stake in the state gas company.
STATE HAS ITS OWN MONEY TO INVEST
The result of all these efforts is that Bahia, unlike virtually all the other states, has its own money to invest.
This year, Souto expects to be able to plough 400 million reais, or about 15 percent of net receipts, into infrastructure. "That is virtually unheard of in Brazil," he said.
In addition, Bahia has used the fact it pays its bills on time to bully contractors into dropping their prices, exceeding by as much as 50 percent its road-building targets in 1996.
Situated in Salvador's modernistic administrative complex, Neto's office is an oasis of efficiency among the pot-holed streets and crumbling buildings of the Bahian capital.
The finance-secretary speaks proudly of his achievements.

"When I took over, I asked for the state's annual tax receipts. I got five different answers, two of them from the same department. Now I can tell you at the touch of a button. We had 34 computers. Now we have 1,400 terminals," he said.

But the contrast between Bahia's fiscal achievements and the reality of life in the streets, where the average salary remains obstinately stuck at minimum wage levels, is ample testimony that balanced books do not always breed economic development.
Bahia is lobbying ferociously for a new federal industrial policy that will entice major manufacturers to the northeast.
Other Brazilian states can only dream of the fiscal health enjoyed by Bahia, despite Brasilia's latest refinancing plan.
In a recent article, the Finance Ministry's Parente acknowledged that adjustment in Rio Grande do Sul will be slow.
Projections are payroll will fall to 70 percent of net annual receipts in 1997 and the state probably will not be able to take out any new debt until the year 2008.

"(But) any analysis must conclude that the situation could not continue, simply because the permanent capitalisation of financial obligations with no amortization would just make the debt stock grow indefinitely, reaching levels completely disproportionate to the state's ability to pay," Parente wrote. ($1=1.02 reai)
